pack.label: Microbiology
pack.description: Organisms, aseptic technique, smears, staining and microscopy. Loops, slides and microscopes live in core; this pack adds organisms, stains and techniques.

techniques.label: Prepare a smear from a liquid culture
techniques.description: Flame the loop, take a loopful of culture onto a slide, flame the loop again, and let the smear air-dry.

quality.statement: The smear holds only the organism from its own culture

errors.statement: The loop is not flamed before or after touching a culture
errors.consequence: Cells ride on the loop into the next culture and onto the next slide (core:transfer, core:sterilise)

techniques.label: Heat-fix a smear
techniques.description: Pass the dried slide through a flame, smear side up, two or three times.

errors.consequence: Each reagent and rinse washes cells off; the slide ends nearly empty (core:flood, core:rinse)

techniques.label: Gram stain
techniques.description: Crystal violet, rinse; Gram's iodine, rinse; decolourise briefly, rinse at once; safranin, rinse; blot dry.

quality.statement: The cells show the colour their Gram class should give

errors.consequence: Gram-positive cells lose crystal violet, take up safranin and look Gram-negative (staining model)
Gram-negative cells keep crystal violet and look Gram-positive (staining model)

techniques.label: Look at a stained slide under the microscope
techniques.description: Find the smear at low power, then add a drop of immersion oil and look with the 100× objective.

techniques.label: Aseptic transfer with a sterile tip
techniques.description: Transfer cells or reagents with a fresh sterile tip, opening tubes only as long as needed.

techniques.label: Recover transformed cells in broth
techniques.description: Add broth to each tube and let the cells recover and start making the resistance protein before plating.

techniques.label: Spread a plate
techniques.description: Pipette the cells onto the agar, sterilise the spreader (ethanol and flame, then let it cool), and spread until the surface is dry.

techniques.label: Incubate plates

techniques.label: Count colonies

techniques.label: Streak a plate for single colonies
techniques.description: Put a loopful of culture in one sector and streak it out; flame the loop and draw each new sector out of the end of the last, four sectors in all.

techniques.description: Flame and cool the loop, touch one well-separated colony, and put the cells into the broth.

techniques.label: Count cells with a haemocytometer and trypan blue
techniques.description: Mix the cells 1:1 with trypan blue, load the chamber, count the four large corner squares (clear and blue cells separately), and work out cells per mL and the proportion alive.

identity.name: EMB base (peptone, lactose, eosin Y, methylene blue)

differential.positive: dark purple-black with a green metallic sheen

provenance.notes: Eosin and methylene blue inhibit Gram-positives; vigorous lactose fermenters that make much acid (E. coli, methyl-red positive) precipitate the dyes with a metallic sheen, other lactose fermenters are pink-purple, non-fermenters colourless.

A soil pseudomonad that degrades alkanes (alk genes) and resists the CFC supplement; oxidase positive. Intrinsically resistant (a chromosomal β-lactamase, efflux, an outer membrane of low permeability) to ampicillin, chloramphenicol and the folate-pathway drugs; susceptible to the aminoglycosides (illustrative MICs).
Suppresses most bacteria other than pseudomonads.
A diesel alkane: a sole carbon source only for organisms that can oxidise alkanes; biosurfactants they make emulsify it, so a culture growing on it goes cloudy.

A sulfonamide: it competes with para-aminobenzoic acid at dihydropteroate synthase, the first committed step of folate synthesis. Bacteriostatic alone. MICs in rich broth such as LB (which supplies thymidine) are high: 16-64 µg/mL for E. coli, 32-128 for S. aureus (illustrative); resistance (sul1, sul2) is a drug-insensitive enzyme.

Inhibits bacterial dihydrofolate reductase, the next step of the folate pathway after the sulfonamides' target; with sulfamethoxazole it is co-trimoxazole. Typical MICs: E. coli about 0.25-0.5 µg/mL, S. aureus about 1 µg/mL (illustrative); resistance (dfrA) is a drug-insensitive enzyme. With sulfamethoxazole the two block successive steps of one pathway: synergy, with a fractional inhibitory concentration index of about 0.3 (illustrative; checkerboard values of 0.1-0.5 are typical).

identity.name: Escherichia coli, urinary isolate carrying dfrA

provenance.notes: Its dfrA gene makes a trimethoprim-insensitive dihydrofolate reductase: resistant far above 8 µg/mL; sulfamethoxazole acts on it as on K-12.
An aminoglycoside: binds the 30S ribosomal subunit and causes misreading; bactericidal. Typical MICs: E. coli 4-8 µg/mL, S. aureus 4-16 (illustrative).
An aminoglycoside (30S subunit); bactericidal and active against pseudomonads. Typical MICs: E. coli 0.25-1 µg/mL, S. aureus 0.12-0.5, P. putida about 1 (illustrative).

A carboxypenicillin: like ampicillin it blocks cell-wall cross-linking and is destroyed by TEM β-lactamase (ampR), but it is more stable in plates and reaches some pseudomonads. Typical MICs: E. coli 4-8 µg/mL, S. aureus about 1 (penicillin-susceptible strains) (illustrative).

identity.name: E. coli BL21(DE3) carrying pET His6-ShPatB

provenance.notes: BL21(DE3), an expression strain with T7 RNA polymerase under lac control, carrying a pET vector (kanamycin resistant). Its proteome is four stand-in host proteins of about 37 fg each per cell.

identity.name: E. coli BL21(DE3) carrying pET His6-GFP

provenance.notes: BL21(DE3), an expression strain with T7 RNA polymerase under lac control, carrying a pET vector (kanamycin resistant). Its proteome is four stand-in host proteins of about 37 fg each per cell.

An Ames tester strain: hisG46 is a missense mutation (proline for leucine) reverted by base-pair substitutions; rfa (a deep-rough outer membrane that lets large molecules in) and ΔuvrB (no excision repair; the deletion runs through bio, so it needs biotin). About 3.4e-17 mol histidine per cell (2.3 % of its protein). Spontaneous revertants about 10-20 per plate (illustrative).
A His⁺ revertant of TA1535: it makes its own histidine again, so it grows into a colony on minimal glucose agar. Still ΔuvrB-bio: it needs biotin.

An Ames tester strain: hisD3052 is a −1 frameshift in a run of repeated CG pairs, reverted by frameshift mutations; rfa and ΔuvrB-bio like TA1535. Spontaneous revertants about 15-30 per plate (illustrative).
A His⁺ revertant of TA1538 (the reading frame restored near the original frameshift). Still needs biotin.
An amino acid: a growth factor for histidine auxotrophs (His⁻ strains).
A vitamin: a growth factor for strains that cannot make it (the Ames strains' uvrB deletion removes bio).

Salmonella turns azide into azidoalanine, which causes base-pair substitutions: it reverts hisG46 (TA1535, TA100) and not frameshift alleles. The usual positive control without liver extract: about 1.5 µg per plate gives a few hundred revertants of TA1535 (potency illustrative). At millimolar levels it kills (it blocks cytochrome oxidase).

A frameshift mutagen that needs no metabolic activation: the usual positive control for TA98 and TA1538 (10-20 µg per plate gives a few hundred revertants; potency illustrative); it does not revert base-substitution alleles. It barely dissolves in water.

A homofermentative lactic acid bacterium of the gut and of probiotic products: long Gram-positive rods in chains, catalase negative, tolerant of acid and acetate, so it grows on MRS. Small rough colonies after two days at 37 °C.
Another probiotic lactobacillus, common in capsules and fermented milks: short Gram-positive rods, grows on MRS with larger, smoother colonies than L. acidophilus.

provenance.notes: A pseudo-substance for the whole base. Rich enough for lactobacilli; its acetate at a low pH (about 5.4 once acidified) holds back most other bacteria, so E. coli does not grow on it.

models.description: Crystal violet retention during decolourisation decays first-order at a rate set by the cell wall and by whether iodine has complexed the dye. Rates are chosen so that about 2–20 s of acetone–ethanol separates the classes; longer turns Gram-positive cells pink, shorter leaves Gram-negative cells purple, and no iodine turns everything pink.

provenance.notes: Teaching-scale rates tuned to the qualitative behaviour, not fitted to measurements.

models.description: Logistic growth with the organism's doubling time, scaled by a cardinal-temperature curve (zero below tMin and above tMax), only where a nutrient is present; antibiotics kill growing cells that lack the resistance marker. On agar, doubling is 1.5× slower and colonies are visible after about 17 doublings; their number is drawn (Poisson) from the viable cells.

provenance.notes: Teaching-scale constants (see models/growth.ts).

models.description: Competent cells bind plasmid DNA on ice (time constant 5 min, saturating with DNA mass); a heat dose above 30 °C during the shock sets the uptake, which peaks at the dose of 50 s at 42 °C and falls for shorter or longer shocks; large doses kill. Lukewarm cells lose competence. Transformants express the plasmid's resistance over about 30 min at 37 °C (slower when cooler), and survive selection by half without it.

provenance.notes: Phenomenological, tuned so the standard protocol gives about 10³ transformants per µg.

models.description: Where contaminants come from in a teaching lab: airborne cells settling on what is uncovered (the bench's rate per cm² per hour), an unflamed rim letting one in on about 4 % of handlings (0.1 % flamed), and fingertips leaving their skin flora (about 150 colonies unwashed, 25 washed, 4 after an antiseptic wipe).

provenance.notes: Teaching-scale values: settle plates in occupied rooms give tens of colonies per 90 mm plate per hour; fingertip press plates give tens to hundreds, reduced by an order of magnitude by washing or alcohol. The rim probabilities are chosen so that careless handling contaminates a fair share of a series of broth transfers and careful handling almost none.

json.title: Gram staining two bacteria
json.summary: Make a smear of each of two broth cultures, heat-fix and Gram stain them, look at them under oil immersion, and classify each organism.
json.briefing: Gram-positive bacteria have a thick peptidoglycan wall that holds the crystal violet–iodine complex when a decolouriser is applied; Gram-negative bacteria lose it and take up the red counterstain. Stain both cultures and decide which is which from what you see.

json.title: Algae in a river: concentrating and counting cells
json.summary: Spin down the algae in 12 mL of water from above, at and below a sewage outfall, take each pellet up in 0.5 mL, count four 1 mm² squares of a haemocytometer twice for each, and work back to cells per mL of river water.
json.briefing: River water holds too few algae to count directly: concentrate them first. Each large corner square of the haemocytometer is 1 mm² under a 0.1 mm coverslip gap, so it holds 0.1 mm³ (10⁻⁴ mL). Cells per mL of the concentrate = mean count per square × 10⁴; divide by the concentration factor for the river. Mix the concentrate just before each load, and count cells touching the top and left lines only.

json.title: Is it safe to swim? Viable counts and faecal indicator bacteria
json.summary: Serially dilute water from two sites, spread nutrient agar for a total viable count and EMB agar for E. coli (green sheen) and other coliforms (pink); count plates of 30–300 colonies, and judge the water against a bathing guideline, knowing what a plate cannot show.
json.briefing: A total viable count on nutrient agar at 37 °C counts what grows there, not everything in the water. E. coli lives in guts and dies off in water, so finding it means recent faecal contamination: on EMB agar it grows dark with a green metallic sheen, while other lactose fermenters are pink-purple and Gram-positives do not grow. Count only plates with 30–300 colonies; bacteria per mL = colonies × dilution factor ÷ 0.1 mL.

json.title: Is it what the label says? Checking two bioremediation cultures
json.summary: Two products are sold as Pseudomonas putida for cleaning up oil-contaminated soil. Gram stain them, grow them on Pseudomonas selective agar, test oxidase, offer them hexadecane as the only carbon source, and run a P. putida-specific PCR on boiled colonies; then decide what each really is.
json.briefing: A bioaugmentation product is only worth adding if it is the organism claimed, and alive. Classical tests narrow the group: Gram-negative rods that are oxidase positive and grow on CFC agar are pseudomonads. Telling species apart needs a test of what this species does (here, growing on an alkane) or of its DNA (primers specific to P. putida, 618 bp). Run controls beside every test.

json.title: Fuel in the soil: counting a degrader by spot plating
json.summary: Four sterile-soil microcosms seeded with an alkane-degrading pseudomonad (with or without an alkane fuel, kept cold or on the bench for a day): suspend half a gram of each, dilute to 10⁻⁶, spot three 10 µL drops of every dilution on one plate, and count the spots two days later to see where the degrader multiplied.
json.briefing: A spot plate puts a whole dilution series on one plate: small drops, each counted on its own. Half a gram of soil in 4.5 mL is a 10⁻¹ suspension (0.1 g of soil per mL), so the colonies in three 10 µL spots of the 10⁻ᵏ tube came from 0.03 mL × 10⁻ᵏ g of soil: cells per gram = colonies ÷ 0.03 × 10ᵏ. Count the most concentrated dilution whose spots still hold separate colonies. Use a fresh tip for each dilution, and put the microcosms back in the fridge once sampled so they do not change.

json.title: A viable count by serial dilution and spread plating
json.summary: Make a ten-fold dilution series of an overnight E. coli culture, spread 100 µL of the 10⁻⁵, 10⁻⁶ and 10⁻⁷ dilutions on duplicate LB plates, incubate overnight, count the plates with 30 to 300 colonies and work out the viable count in CFU per mL.
json.briefing: Each colony grew from one viable cell (a colony-forming unit). Too many colonies merge and too few give a poor estimate, so count only plates with 30 to 300 colonies. CFU/mL = colonies ÷ (volume plated × dilution).

json.title: The minimum inhibitory concentration of ampicillin
json.summary: Make two-fold dilutions of ampicillin from 128 to 0.25 µg/mL across a 96-well plate, inoculate one row with a susceptible E. coli and one with an unknown strain, incubate overnight, read the turbidity at 600 nm and find each strain's MIC.
json.briefing: The MIC is the lowest concentration that stops visible growth overnight. Each well has half the drug of the one before it. The growth control (no drug) must be turbid and the sterility control (no cells) clear, or the plate cannot be read. A strain whose MIC is above the clinical breakpoint (8 µg/mL here) is resistant.

json.title: Identifying an unknown bacterium
json.summary: Identify an unknown culture, one of five teaching organisms, from its Gram stain, a catalase test, an oxidase test and its growth and colour on MacConkey agar.
json.briefing: Work down the key: Gram stain first (and the cells' shape), then catalase (hydrogen peroxide: bubbles if positive) and oxidase (purple within 10 s if positive). MacConkey agar lets only Gram-negatives grow, and lactose fermenters turn pink on it. The candidates are Escherichia coli, Pseudomonas fluorescens, Staphylococcus aureus, Micrococcus luteus and Lactococcus lactis.

json.title: Antibiotic susceptibility by disc diffusion
json.summary: Seed Mueller–Hinton plates with standardised suspensions of E. coli, S. aureus and an unknown isolate, press on ampicillin, tetracycline, kanamycin and chloramphenicol discs, incubate overnight, measure the inhibition zones and classify the isolate.
json.briefing: A disc's antibiotic spreads into the agar while the lawn grows; where the drug reaches the MIC before the lawn is established, nothing grows. A smaller MIC gives a larger zone, so the zone diameter reads the organism's susceptibility. The test only works standardised: a 0.5 McFarland inoculum (about 1.5 × 10⁸ CFU/mL), agar 4 mm deep, discs on within 15 minutes, 16–20 h at 35–37 °C. This course's breakpoints for ampicillin (10 µg) on Enterobacterales: susceptible ≥ 17 mm, intermediate 14–16 mm, resistant ≤ 13 mm. They are illustrative; real testing uses the current CLSI or EUCAST tables.

json.title: Microbes everywhere: where contamination comes from, and keeping it out
json.summary: Leave plates open to the air for different times and press fingertips on agar before and after washing; pass loopfuls between sterile broths with flamed necks beside an unopened control; plate pond water at two temperatures; stab two cultures into agar deeps. Two days later, count, look and explain.
json.briefing: Anything uncovered collects what settles out of the air, and anything you touch collects what is on your skin. Aseptic technique keeps both out: open vessels only briefly, flame the neck of a bottle or tube after opening it and before closing it, flame the loop before and after each use. Count only plates with separate colonies.
